title: Superdry strategic analysis
text:
About the project
Our group of six acted as a consulting firm, A & A Consultancy, tasked with producing a full strategic review of Superdry, the British apparel brand that rose to become a FTSE-listed retailer and then collapsed into retrenchment and delisting. The report examined how the brand captured value in its early years, why it declined through overexpansion and brand dilution, and what strategic interventions could restore its competitive position.
The analysis followed a structured consulting process of Orientation, Diagnostics, Intervention, Evaluation, applying frameworks including PESTEL, Porter’s Five Forces, SWOT, RBV/VRIO, the Strategy Diamond and the ERRC Grid. As Associate Director I led analysis and synthesis work particularly across the Diagnostics and Evaluation stages, with input from the team across every section. The group built the underlying insights; this page rebuilds the key visual artefacts as interactive Plotly and Mermaid renders for the portfolio.






NoteWhat’s on this page



The visualisations below reproduce the core strategic artefacts from the Group BS1 Superdry report. Financial data comes from Superdry’s publicly reported annual accounts (FY2014 to FY2024); the framework scoring reflects our group’s consensus diagnostic rather than external research. The original report used static exhibits; this page rebuilds the same underlying analysis as executable Python with Plotly, plus Mermaid for the conceptual diagrams, as a portfolio extension.

title: Superdry strategic analysis
text:
1. The decline in numbers
Superdry’s financial trajectory tells the story more clearly than any framework. Revenue more than doubled between FY2014 and FY2018 as the brand rode its Japanese-Americana aesthetic to global expansion. From the FY2018 peak onward, decline was continuous through a combination of brand dilution, perpetual discounting, structural retail pressure, and the pandemic. By FY2024 revenue had fallen to roughly 56% of its peak, and the company was taken private that July1.


Code
import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go

revenue_history = pd.DataFrame({
    "Year":    ["FY14", "FY15", "FY16", "FY17", "FY18", "FY19", "FY20", "FY21", "FY22", "FY23", "FY24"],
    "Revenue": [430,    486,    590,    752,    872,    872,    705,    556,    610,    622,    488],
    "Phase":   ["Growth", "Growth", "Growth", "Growth", "Peak", "Peak",
                "Decline", "Decline", "Stabilisation", "Stabilisation", "Retrenchment"],
})

phase_colours = {
    "Growth": "#1e7e34",
    "Peak": "#d4a017",
    "Decline": "#c8102e",
    "Stabilisation": "#4a90a4",
    "Retrenchment": "#6c757d",
}

fig = go.Figure()

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=revenue_history["Year"],
    y=revenue_history["Revenue"],
    mode="lines+markers",
    line=dict(color="#1a1a1a", width=2.5),
    marker=dict(
        size=11,
        color=[phase_colours[p] for p in revenue_history["Phase"]],
        line=dict(color="white", width=1.5),
    ),
    text=[f"£{v}m" for v in revenue_history["Revenue"]],
    hovertemplate="<b>%{x}</b><br>Revenue: %{text}<br>Phase: %{customdata}<extra></extra>",
    customdata=revenue_history["Phase"],
    showlegend=False,
))

fig.add_annotation(x="FY18", y=872, text="<b>Peak</b><br>£872m",
                   showarrow=True, arrowhead=2, arrowcolor="#d4a017",
                   ax=0, ay=-40, font=dict(size=11, color="#1a1a1a"))
fig.add_annotation(x="FY21", y=556, text="<b>Trough</b><br>Covid + dilution",
                   showarrow=True, arrowhead=2, arrowcolor="#c8102e",
                   ax=40, ay=30, font=dict(size=11, color="#1a1a1a"))
fig.add_annotation(x="FY24", y=488, text="<b>Taken private</b><br>July 2024",
                   showarrow=True, arrowhead=2, arrowcolor="#6c757d",
                   ax=-30, ay=-50, font=dict(size=11, color="#1a1a1a"))

for phase, colour in phase_colours.items():
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[None], y=[None], mode="markers",
        marker=dict(size=10, color=colour),
        name=phase, showlegend=True,
    ))

fig.update_layout(
    height=460,
    margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=30, b=30),
    paper_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    plot_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    font=dict(family="Inter, sans-serif", color="#1a1a1a"),
    xaxis=dict(showgrid=False),
    yaxis=dict(title="Revenue (£ millions)", showgrid=True, gridcolor="#eee", range=[350, 950]),
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02, x=0),

Figure 1: Superdry annual revenue, FY2014 to FY2024. The brand doubled revenue in four years to an FY2018 peak of roughly £872m, then lost the majority of that growth over the following six years. The company was taken private in July 2024.




The five phases shown above map directly onto the strategic narrative of the report: an early Growth period built on differentiated brand identity, a Peak where over-expansion and licensing began diluting the equity, a Decline accelerated by pandemic demand shifts and the cost-of-living crisis, a Stabilisation as the founder returned and discounting was reduced, and the current Retrenchment back to core markets.

title: Superdry strategic analysis
text:
2. Industry attractiveness: Porter’s Five Forces
Applying Porter’s Five Forces to the apparel sector shows why Superdry’s current mid-market position is structurally exposed. Four of the five forces register at High or Medium-High intensity. The scoring below is our group’s consensus assessment from the Diagnostics stage, with supporting logic in the report.


Code
import plotly.graph_objects as go

forces = pd.DataFrame({
    "Force": [
        "Competitive rivalry",
        "Buyer power",
        "Threat of substitutes",
        "Threat of new entrants",
        "Supplier power",
    ],
    "Score": [5, 5, 5, 4, 3],
    "Evidence": [
        "Fast fashion (Shein, Boohoo), sportswear giants (Nike, Adidas), heritage revival (Barbour)",
        "Low switching costs, price transparency, loyalty shift from brand to value",
        "Athleisure, second-hand markets, rental services",
        "E-commerce lowers barriers but brand equity still hard to build",
        "Moderate concentration in global apparel supply chains",
    ],
})

fig = go.Figure()

fig.add_trace(go.Scatterpolar(
    r=list(forces["Score"]) + [forces["Score"].iloc[0]],
    theta=list(forces["Force"]) + [forces["Force"].iloc[0]],
    fill="toself",
    fillcolor="rgba(200,16,46,0.20)",
    line=dict(color="#c8102e", width=2.5),
    marker=dict(size=10, color="#c8102e"),
    text=forces["Evidence"].tolist() + [forces["Evidence"].iloc[0]],
    hovertemplate="<b>%{theta}</b><br>Intensity: %{r}/5<br>%{text}<extra></extra>",
    name="Force intensity",
))

fig.update_layout(
    polar=dict(
        radialaxis=dict(visible=True, range=[0, 5], tickvals=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
                        ticktext=["1", "2", "3", "4", "5"],
                        gridcolor="#ddd", linecolor="#ddd"),
        angularaxis=dict(gridcolor="#ddd", linecolor="#ddd"),
        bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    ),
    height=480,
    margin=dict(l=60, r=60, t=30, b=30),
    paper_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    font=dict(family="Inter, sans-serif", color="#1a1a1a"),
    showlegend=False,
)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 2: Porter’s Five Forces acting on Superdry. Scores from 1 (low intensity) to 5 (high intensity) reflect the Group BS1 diagnostic assessment. Four of the five forces sit at high or medium-high intensity, giving an overall low industry attractiveness for an undifferentiated mid-market player.




The implication is blunt: Superdry cannot win by trying to out-compete Shein on price or Nike on scale. A mid-market undifferentiated player in this industry structure has no natural profit pool. Either re-establish meaningful differentiation or continue margin compression indefinitely.

title: Superdry strategic analysis
text:
3. The Value Stick, shortened
The Value Stick concept frames strategic value capture as the vertical distance between a customer’s willingness to pay (WTP) at the top and the firm’s cost at the bottom, with price sitting in between. A healthy brand runs a long stick: high WTP, controlled costs, room for both consumer surplus and firm margin.
Superdry’s decline can be read cleanly on this frame. Between 2012 and 2023, WTP compressed (the brand lost its premium cachet), costs rose (through discounting, logistics complexity and wholesale dilution), and the stick shortened dramatically.


Code
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("<b>2012: Peak Superdry</b>", "<b>2023: Diluted brand</b>"),
                    horizontal_spacing=0.2)

peak_wtp, peak_price, peak_cost = 100, 70, 35

fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=["Peak"], y=[peak_cost], name="Cost",
                     marker=dict(color="#6c757d"), showlegend=True,
                     text=f"£{peak_cost}", textposition="inside",
                     textfont=dict(color="white", size=14)), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=["Peak"], y=[peak_price - peak_cost], name="Firm margin",
                     marker=dict(color="#1e7e34"), showlegend=True,
                     text=f"£{peak_price - peak_cost}", textposition="inside",
                     textfont=dict(color="white", size=14)), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=["Peak"], y=[peak_wtp - peak_price], name="Consumer surplus",
                     marker=dict(color="#c8e6c9"), showlegend=True,
                     text=f"£{peak_wtp - peak_price}", textposition="inside",
                     textfont=dict(color="#1a1a1a", size=14)), row=1, col=1)

dil_wtp, dil_price, dil_cost = 55, 40, 32

fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=["Diluted"], y=[dil_cost], name="Cost",
                     marker=dict(color="#6c757d"), showlegend=False,
                     text=f"£{dil_cost}", textposition="inside",
                     textfont=dict(color="white", size=14)), row=1, col=2)
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=["Diluted"], y=[dil_price - dil_cost], name="Firm margin",
                     marker=dict(color="#1e7e34"), showlegend=False,
                     text=f"£{dil_price - dil_cost}", textposition="inside",
                     textfont=dict(color="white", size=14)), row=1, col=2)
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=["Diluted"], y=[dil_wtp - dil_price], name="Consumer surplus",
                     marker=dict(color="#c8e6c9"), showlegend=False,
                     text=f"£{dil_wtp - dil_price}", textposition="inside",
                     textfont=dict(color="#1a1a1a", size=14)), row=1, col=2)

fig.add_annotation(x="Peak", y=peak_wtp, text=f"<b>WTP £{peak_wtp}</b>",
                   showarrow=False, yshift=14, font=dict(size=12, color="#1a1a1a"), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_annotation(x="Diluted", y=dil_wtp, text=f"<b>WTP £{dil_wtp}</b>",
                   showarrow=False, yshift=14, font=dict(size=12, color="#1a1a1a"), row=1, col=2)

fig.update_layout(
    barmode="stack",
    height=480,
    margin=dict(l=40, r=40, t=50, b=30),
    paper_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    plot_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    font=dict(family="Inter, sans-serif", color="#1a1a1a"),
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=-0.12, x=0.25),
)
fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 115], showgrid=True, gridcolor="#eee", title="£")
fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=False)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 3: The Value Stick concept applied to Superdry. Left: peak 2012 positioning with strong WTP, controlled cost base and visible margin. Right: 2023 after dilution, with compressed WTP, higher effective costs and negligible margin. Figures are illustrative to show the directional shift.




The key observation is that margin (green) shrinks sharply even though the firm lowered price. Cost did not fall proportionately because discounting behaviour, wholesale concessions and licensing overheads added hidden complexity. This is the vicious cycle described in the report’s Diagnostics section: low-margin, volume-based economic logic that destroys brand value and profitability simultaneously.

title: Superdry strategic analysis
text:
4. SWOT synthesis
The internal analysis surfaced a stark gap between genuine residual strengths (brand recognition, design archive, founder-led creative direction) and acute weaknesses (brand dilution, weak digital, high-cost legacy model, debt overhang). The matrix below summarises the full SWOT from the report.

  

    
      Strengths
      
        Global brand recognition
        Distinctive design DNA
        Founder-led creative direction restored
        Established retail presence
      
    

    
      Weaknesses
      
        Severe brand dilution from over-licensing
        Perpetual discounting eroding equity
        Weak digital and DTC capabilities
        Wholesale-reliant high-cost model
        Crippling debt burden
      
    

    
      Opportunities
      
        Sustainability / circular fashion
        Digital transformation & DTC
        Refocus core markets & categories
        Experiential retail using heritage
      
    

    
      Threats
      
        Fierce competition (Shein, Nike)
        Higher sustainability expectations
        Cost-of-living pressure on premium
        Heritage strategy risks becoming dated
      
    

  
  Figure 4: Superdry SWOT matrix

Viewed as a diagnostic rather than an inventory, the SWOT makes two points clear. First, the strengths are heritage assets: real but finite, and they depreciate fast without investment. Second, the weaknesses and threats reinforce each other (perpetual discounting plus cost-of-living pressure plus weak digital plus fierce competition form a trap). Any renewal strategy has to break that reinforcing loop.

title: Superdry strategic analysis
section: 5. Strategy Diamond: where the trade-offs went wrong
text:
5. Strategy Diamond: where the trade-offs went wrong
Hambrick and Fredrickson’s Strategy Diamond frames a strategy as five interlocking elements that must reinforce each other: Arenas, Vehicles, Differentiators, Staging, and Economic Logic. The report’s Diagnostics section used the Diamond to synthesise Superdry’s historical mis-steps into a single integrated picture.



  
  
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
  

  
  
  Arenas
  Chose global mass-market
  over focused core

  
  
  Vehicles
  Wholesale + licensing
  over DTC control

  
  
  Differentiators
  Traded design identity
  for ubiquity

  
  
  Staging
  Blitz-scale before
  operations ready

  
  
  Economic logic
  Premium → low-margin
  volume-based model

  
  
  Economic logic
  is the hinge element


  Figure 5: Strategy Diamond applied to Superdry's historical strategy. Each element traded away its original strength, and the elements ceased to reinforce each other.








TipThe Economic Logic element is the hinge



All four other elements can be fixed tactically. The Economic Logic shift from premium value-based to low-margin volume-based is the one that structurally reset the cost base, and unwinding it requires rebuilding willingness to pay first. That sequencing is what the report’s Evaluation section addresses through the phased roadmap below.

title: Superdry strategic analysis
text:
Reflection
This was my first experience working in a consulting format with a formally defined team structure and a real business case. The most valuable lesson was learning how frameworks that look mechanical on the page (PESTEL, Five Forces, Strategy Diamond) function very differently when applied to an actual declining company with incomplete information. The Strategy Diamond in particular was initially treated by the group as a five-box summary exercise and only became useful when we started arguing about which of the five elements was the hinge. That debate (which we eventually resolved on the Economic Logic element) was the point at which our analysis graduated from description into diagnosis.
The group dynamics were the other major learning. We hit a rough patch around the in-module presentation, where last-minute slide changes combined with IT issues produced a coordination failure that was uncomfortable at the time. Working through it afterwards, with a combination of honest conversation and shared resolve to make the report itself a strong piece of work, taught me more about managing team pressure than the frameworks themselves did. The skills matrix we drew up early in the project (a consulting tool I had not encountered before) turned out to be the single most useful organisational device we used, because it gave each member a defensible domain and reduced duplication.
Reproducing the analytical exhibits as interactive Python and Mermaid renders for this portfolio was a separate exercise from the module itself. The original report used static diagrams embedded in a designed PDF. Rebuilding them forced me to re-examine whether each framework actually added unique insight, or whether some were decorative rather than diagnostic. The Porter’s Five Forces radar and the Value Stick are, on reflection, the two frameworks that pulled the most analytical weight in the final argument. The others supported that argument rather than producing it independently.
Strategy as a discipline is less about running more frameworks and more about choosing the two or three that matter for the specific question, then applying them rigorously enough to produce a decision. That was the takeaway I carried out of the module, and it is the lens I intend to apply to business analytics roles where the risk is usually the same: too many dashboards, not enough diagnosis.

title: Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention
text:
About the research
This was my final research paper for the BAA1027 Machine Learning module, supervised by Dr Michael Farayola. Unlike my group projects, this was a solo piece of work from dataset selection through to final submission. The dataset is the Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention collection published by Sakar et al. (2019) and distributed through the UCI Machine Learning Repository: 12,330 online sessions described by 17 features and a binary Revenue target, with a moderate 15.5% positive class imbalance.
The research question was whether a standard comparative classifier pipeline could be meaningfully extended by three additions: K-means cluster labels injected as an engineered feature, a soft voting ensemble, and cost-sensitive threshold optimisation parameterised from published e-commerce economics. The empirical answer, reported honestly including the two innovations that did not work, produced a more interesting finding than if everything had worked: the decision rule matters more than the classifier.






NoteWhat’s on this page



The sections below reproduce the core findings of the research paper as executable Python with Plotly. The original notebook used matplotlib and seaborn in Google Colab; this page rebuilds the same underlying analysis as interactive charts for the portfolio. Click the </> Code button at the top to toggle all source code, or unfold any single chunk to inspect it. All numerical results originate from the executed notebook submitted for assessment.

title: Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention
text:
1. Classifier benchmark
Five classifiers were tuned via GridSearchCV with 5-fold stratified cross-validation, scoring on F1 rather than accuracy to reflect the class imbalance. XGBoost recorded the highest F1 (66.73%) and PR-AUC (74.53%), narrowly ahead of Random Forest. SVM and Logistic Regression lagged materially, the former on recall, the latter because a linear decision surface cannot model the non-linear PageValues saturation effect.

Figure 1: Classification metrics across the five tuned models. XGBoost wins on F1 and PR-AUC; the Voting Classifier wins on precision but loses recall, producing a lower F1 than XGBoost alone.




The Voting Classifier illustrates a counterintuitive result: it aggregates the four base learners via soft probability voting and achieves the highest precision of any model (77.64%), but it loses recall relative to XGBoost alone (44.93% vs 61.36%). The net effect is an F1 of 56.92%, ten points below XGBoost. Cornelio et al. (2021) show that voting ensembles produce marginal gains only when base learners have complementary failure modes. On this dataset they do not, so the ensemble is reported as a negative result rather than buried in the appendix.

2. Generalisation: XGBoost vs Random Forest
On headline test-set F1, XGBoost and Random Forest look comparable. The train versus test comparison tells a materially different story. Random Forest achieved a perfect training F1 of 1.000 against a test F1 of 0.621, a 0.38 gap indicating severe overfitting despite the F1-scored grid search. XGBoost, by contrast, produced a 0.04 gap between training and test performance.

The Random Forest grid search converged on unlimited max_depth and single-sample leaves, which explains the perfect training fit. In a production setting, tighter regularisation via a constrained depth search or a higher min_samples_split would be worth exploring. For the purposes of this paper, the clean XGBoost gap argues for it as the production model of choice regardless of the narrow test-set margin.

text:
3. The cost-sensitive threshold innovation
This is the paper’s central methodological contribution and its strongest empirical result. The default 0.5 classification threshold presumes symmetric misclassification costs, which is rarely appropriate in e-commerce. I derived a cost ratio from two published benchmarks: Littledata (2025) reports USD 92 average revenue per Shopify customer; WordStream (2025) reports USD 19.68 average Facebook Ads cost per acquisition. The ratio of 4.67 was rounded up to 5 to reflect a deliberate preference toward minority-class recall, then stress-tested across the 3:1 to 7:1 range.

Two results emerge from the sensitivity analysis. First, the optimal threshold is stable at 0.16 across ratios 3:1 through 6:1, shifting only modestly to 0.11 at 7:1. The threshold optimisation is robust to moderate misspecification of the cost ratio, which matters because the Littledata and WordStream benchmarks are US-based while the dataset is of unknown geography. Second, the cost reduction scales monotonically from 16.5% at the most conservative ratio to 41.9% at the most aggressive. Even at 3:1 the adjustment delivers double-digit savings.


Code
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

# Illustrative curve reconstructed from the paper's cost function
# Total cost = 5 * FN + 1 * FP under the 5:1 cost ratio
thresholds = np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, 91)

# Smooth U-shape with minimum around 0.16, calibrated to paper figures
# Default (0.5) cost = 1234, optimum (0.16) cost = 825
def cost_curve(t):
    base = 825 + 3200 * (t - 0.16) ** 2
    if t < 0.16:
        base += 2400 * (0.16 - t) ** 1.4
    return base

costs = np.array([cost_curve(t) for t in thresholds])

fig = go.Figure()

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=thresholds, y=costs,

This is the basis for the paper’s central argument: for imbalanced business classification problems, the translation of business economics into a decision rule delivers more practitioner value than incremental improvements in classifier accuracy.

4. What the threshold shift actually does
The cost reduction on its own is a summary statistic. The confusion-matrix shift underneath it shows the operational trade-off: at the optimal threshold the model catches far more positive cases but at the price of more false alarms. This is the right trade-off for an e-commerce retargeting use case where the cost of missing a potential converter (lost revenue) substantially exceeds the cost of showing an advert to a non-converter.

The key cell is the false-negative count. At the default threshold, 221 genuine buyers were classified as non-buyers, representing either missed retargeting opportunities or under-prioritised sessions in a live recommendation system. At the optimal threshold that figure drops to 82, recovering 139 previously misclassified converters. The cost of doing so is 286 additional false positives, but under the 5:1 cost ratio this is a favourable trade by design.

title: Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention
text:
Limitations acknowledged in the paper






WarningFour limitations worth flagging




Single platform, single time window. The dataset reflects one e-commerce platform and a twelve-month collection window, which constrains generalisability.
Geographical mismatch on the cost ratio. The Littledata and WordStream benchmarks are US-based, while the dataset geography is unknown. The sensitivity analysis in Section 3 directly mitigates this concern by showing threshold stability across 3:1 to 7:1.
Single stratified split. Evaluation relies on one train/test partition, leaving metrics subject to sampling variance. k-fold test evaluation would tighten confidence intervals.
Scaler fitted on full dataset. The MinMaxScaler was applied to the full frame before the train/test split rather than fitted on the training partition only. The deterministic bounded nature of Min-Max scaling makes material impact unlikely, but the pattern should be corrected in production.

title: Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention
text:
Reflection
This was the most technically demanding piece of work of my degree. The core lesson was methodological rather than technical. Going into the project I expected the interesting finding to be which classifier won. What actually emerged was that the classifier choice mattered much less than the decision rule applied on top of it. The 33.1% cost reduction from the threshold shift is larger than the F1 gap between any two classifiers in the baseline comparison, which is a result I did not anticipate and which changed how I think about applied machine learning.
Reporting the two negative results honestly was a deliberate choice and the one that took most intellectual adjustment. K-means cluster injection and the soft voting ensemble were both methodologically defensible ideas when I designed them. Neither worked. The temptation to either bury them in the appendix or find a metric that made them look marginally favourable was real. Instead I kept them in the main narrative with an explicit framing as negative results and a reasoned explanation of why they failed (the tree ensembles had already extracted the available signal from the raw features, and the base learners lacked the complementary failure modes that voting ensembles depend on). Reading the resulting paper back, the negative results strengthen rather than weaken the overall argument, because they locate the positive result (cost-sensitive thresholding) more precisely in methodological space.
The broader takeaway I carried out of the module is that machine learning as a discipline is closer to applied statistics with a business objective than to computer science with a model zoo. The classifier is the smaller part of the problem. The decision rule, the evaluation design, the limitation audit and the feature interpretability are the parts that determine whether the model is useful or misleading. This is the lens I intend to apply in business analyst roles where similar risks apply: accuracy-optimising a model against a dataset that is not the real production distribution is the easiest way to produce an impressive-looking artefact that fails in deployment.

title: PriceBeo
text:
About the project
PriceBeo is a mobile app that lets users scan any product barcode in-store and instantly compare prices across Ireland’s five major retailers: Tesco, Dunnes Stores, Lidl, Aldi and SuperValu. With grocery prices up 27% since 20211 and limited tools available to Irish shoppers, the app targets a clear and validated market gap.
As CTO, my role was to lead the technical vision and strategy for the platform, translate between the business team and technical advisors, and make informed architecture decisions. I contributed the analytical spine with input from the team across the sections below. The group then built that analysis into the investor-ready report and pitch deck.






NoteWhat’s on this page



The sections below reproduce the core analytics from the PriceBeo business plan as executable Python with Plotly. The original pitch used static exhibits; this page rebuilds the same underlying model interactively for the portfolio. Every chart is generated live from the numbers in the business report. Click the </> Code button at the top of the page to toggle all source code, or unfold any single chunk to inspect it.

Ireland’s grocery market is worth approximately €13 billion a year and is highly concentrated. The top five retailers capture 92.3% of spend, leaving 7.7% for everyone else2. text:
5. Unit economics
The financial projections live or die on unit economics. For a freemium SaaS-style business the core question is not “how much revenue”, it is whether each acquired Premium user generates enough lifetime value to cover acquisition cost.






NoteThe two numbers that matter



Customer acquisition cost (CAC): €1.31. Calculated from total Year 1 marketing spend (€19,700) divided by acquired users (15,000 MAU).
Lifetime value (LTV): depends on retention. Industry consumer-app benchmarks suggest 12 to 24 months typical retention for a freemium utility with weekly use cases. PriceBeo’s weekly shop cadence places it at the high end.


The calculation below is an extension I built for this portfolio to stress-test the LTV assumption across three retention scenarios. The €1.31 CAC and 92% gross margin come from the original financial model; the sensitivity analysis itself was not in the pitch but is a natural follow-on to the numbers the model produces.


Code
import pandas as pd

price_per_month  = 2.99
gross_margin     = 0.92
cac              = 1.31
retention_scenarios = {"Conservative (12 mo)": 12, "Base case (18 mo)": 18, "Optimistic (24 mo)": 24}

rows = []
for name, months_retained in retention_scenarios.items():
    ltv = price_per_month * months_retained * gross_margin
    rows.append({
        "Scenario": name,
        "Retention (months)": months_retained,
        "LTV (€)": round(ltv, 2),
        "LTV:CAC ratio": f"{ltv / cac:.1f}x",
        "Months to recover CAC": round(cac / (price_per_month * gross_margin), 2),
    })

economics = pd.DataFrame(rows)

8. Technical architecture
As CTO my core contribution was validating that the technical model was feasible at the price point the financials required. PriceBeo runs on a stateless REST API fronting a PostgreSQL database that holds the barcode-indexed product catalogue and retailer price feeds. Scans run through Google ML Kit on-device, which avoids round-trip latency and keeps the scan-to-result time under two seconds.

text:
Reflection
PriceBeo was the most demanding and rewarding project of my degree. Working across four assignments over the full academic year, the project developed my ability to think like a founder: validating a real problem, designing a technically sound solution, building a financial model that survives scrutiny and pitching to investors under time pressure.
The most valuable lesson was learning to hold technical decisions and commercial realities in tension at the same time. As CTO I repeatedly had to choose between technically cleaner architectures and commercially sensible ones. The PostgreSQL decision is a good example: a NoSQL document store would have been faster to build, but PostgreSQL’s strict schema gave the data accuracy guarantees the consumer trust narrative depended on. That kind of trade-off does not exist in a module exercise with a single optimisation target. It only emerges when technical, financial and brand decisions sit in the same meeting.
Building the analytical sections on this page was a separate exercise from the module itself. The original pitch used static exhibits in a PowerPoint deck; reproducing the same underlying model as executable Python with Plotly for this portfolio forced me to revisit every assumption end-to-end. Several numbers I had taken for granted during the module needed to be reconstructed from the source spreadsheet, which turned into a useful audit of the financial model’s internal consistency.
The Dragons Den pitch itself was a genuine test of composure under pressure. Reconstructing the full analytical backbone as a standalone, interactive page, rather than as static PDF exhibits, has given me an output I can genuinely point recruiters at.
